steps.body:
The tangent is a good stand-in **near a**, and a bad one far from it. Two things ruin the approximation:

**Distance.** The error grows roughly like (x − a)².
**Curvature.** The bigger |f″|, the faster the curve peels away from its tangent.

So the error is governed by f″ — the same function that told you which SIDE the error was on.

explanationVariants: The error behaves like (x − a)², so DOUBLING the distance quadruples it — a linear approximation degrades quadratically.
That is why the tangent is superb at 9.1 and worthless at 25.

widget.prompt: The error in a linear approximation grows like (x − a)². If you double the distance from a, roughly what happens to the error?

options.label: It quadruples.
options.feedback: Right — squaring the distance squares the error. Move twice as far and pay four times the price.

options.label: It doubles.
options.feedback: That would be a LINEAR error growth. The (x − a)² says the error is quadratic in the distance.

options.label: It stays the same.
options.feedback: The tangent and the curve diverge steadily. Distance is precisely what ruins the approximation.

options.label: It halves.
options.feedback: Errors do not shrink as you move AWAY from the point of tangency.

widget.prompt: On y = x², squeeze the gap and watch the secant merge with the tangent — then think about what happens when the gap is LARGE.
widget.successFeedback: Close in, the secant and the tangent are indistinguishable — which is exactly why linearisation works near a. But look back at the wide gaps: there the secant and the tangent were far apart, and a tangent-based estimate over that range would have been badly wrong. Local means LOCAL.
widget.lowFeedback: At a gap of exactly 0 the quotient is 0/0. Come back a hair — the tangent lives arbitrarily close to a, never at nothing.
widget.highFeedback: The gap is still wide, so the secant cuts across the curve rather than grazing it — which is the picture of a linearisation used too far from home.

predict.prompt: You'll squeeze the gap h toward 0, dragging B into A at x = 3. What does the secant's slope do?
predict.reveal: The secant slopes home in on 6 — the tangent slope at x = 3. A derivative is not a new kind of slope; it is the number the secant slopes were already approaching.

cml.actionGoal: Shrink the interval between two points and compare secant slope with the limiting tangent slope.

explanationVariants: Near a sharp bend, |f″| is large, so the curve leaves its tangent almost immediately. The linearisation is only trustworthy over a very small range.
A nearly-straight curve (small |f″|) can be linearised over a wide range; a violently curved one cannot.

widget.prompt: Two curves are linearised at the same point. One has |f″| = 0.01, the other |f″| = 100. Which linearisation is trustworthy over a wider range?

options.label: The curve with |f″| = 0.01.
options.feedback: Right. Curvature is exactly what makes a curve leave its tangent, and a curve that barely bends barely leaves.

options.label: The curve with |f″| = 100.
options.feedback: That curve bends violently, so it peels away from the tangent almost immediately. Its linearisation is trustworthy only very close in.

options.label: Both are equally reliable.
options.feedback: The error is proportional to |f″|. A hundred-fold difference in curvature is a hundred-fold difference in error.

options.label: Neither is locally reliable.
options.feedback: Both work — near enough to a. The question is only how NEAR is near enough, and f″ answers it.

steps.body:
There is one more way for it to fail, and it is fatal:

**If f is not differentiable at a, there is no tangent to use.**

No tangent, no linearisation. |x| at 0 has no linear approximation at all — you cannot approximate a corner with a line and expect it to work on both sides.

explanationVariants: |x| has no derivative at 0 — the left slope is −1 and the right is +1 — so there is no tangent line, and nothing to linearise WITH.
Every linearisation begins with f′(a). If that number does not exist, the method never starts.

widget.prompt: Why can f(x) = |x| not be linearised at x = 0?

options.label: No derivative exists at x = 0.
options.feedback: Right. L(x) = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a) needs f′(a), and at a corner that number does not exist.

options.label: It is discontinuous at x = 0.
options.feedback: It is perfectly continuous. The failure is in the SLOPE, not the value — which is exactly the distinction C1 drew.

options.label: Its value is 0 at x = 0.
options.feedback: A zero value causes no trouble at all. Plenty of functions are linearised at points where they vanish.

options.label: Its tangent has slope 0.
options.feedback: Averaging the two one-sided slopes is not something the definition permits, and the resulting line fits neither side of the corner.

steps.body: How far can you trust it?
hints: The estimate of √9.1 was out by about 0.00005 — the distance from a was 0.1.
The error grows like (x − a)². Going from 0.1 to 1.0 multiplies the distance by 10.
So the error is multiplied by 10² = 100.
explanationVariants: Ten times the distance means about a hundred times the error: roughly 0.005 instead of 0.00005.
And that is still surprisingly good — √10 ≈ 3.1623, and the tangent gives 3 + 1/6 ≈ 3.1667, out by 0.0044. The quadratic rule predicted it almost exactly.

widget.prompt: The linear estimate of √9.1 was out by about 0.00005. Roughly how many times bigger is the error for √10 (ten times further from a = 9)?

commonErrors.feedback: The error grows like the SQUARE of the distance. Ten times the distance means 10² = 100 times the error.
Doubling would be a linear error law. The (x − a)² makes it quadratic.
That would be a cubic law. The error goes like the square: 10² = 100.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Error ~ (x − a)², so 10× the distance gives 100× the error — about 0.005, and the true error is 0.0044.

takeaways: The error grows like (x − a)²: double the distance and you quadruple the error.
It is proportional to |f″| — the curvature is what pulls the curve away from its tangent.
No derivative, no tangent, no linearisation. A corner cannot be approximated by a line.
steps.teaser: Last chapter: the 0/0 form from precalculus, finally explained.

concept.body: Two questions before you trust a linearisation. **How far from a am I?** (the error grows like the square of that distance) and **how hard does the curve bend?** (the error is proportional to |f″|). Close in and gently curved: excellent. Far out and sharply curved: useless.

explanationVariants: 9.1 is very close to 9, so the tangent is excellent there. 16 is far away, and the estimate would be poor.

widget.prompt: Using the tangent to √x at x = 9, which estimate is more trustworthy?

options.feedback: Right — it is only 0.1 from the base point, so the error is tiny.
That is 7 units from a = 9. The error grows like the square of the distance, so it is far less reliable.
